name: Hydrochlorothiazide

lead: Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) is a widely prescribed water pill that some forum users discuss as a milder, daily alternative to stronger loop diuretics for a less puffy, more defined face.

It blocks the sodium-chloride cotransporter in the kidney, so less sodium and water are reabsorbed and more leave in the urine. Effects start within about 2 hours and last roughly 6-12 hours. It has been sold since 1959 and is used for high blood pressure and fluid retention; no clinical study has tested it for facial puffiness.

paras: It is a prescription tablet, usually taken once daily in its medical use. In forum discussion it is framed as a gentler everyday option compared with furosemide, with the water-loss effect starting the same day.

Documented effects include low potassium, sodium and magnesium, high uric acid and calcium, raised blood sugar and lipids, and sun sensitivity. Regulators in Australia and the US highlighted a link to non-melanoma skin cancer in 2020. It is prescription-only and prohibited by WADA.

angle.text: Some forum users take hydrochlorothiazide as a daily water pill aimed at a less puffy, more defined face. It makes the kidneys excrete more sodium and water, so less fluid is retained. It is a common blood-pressure drug and has not been studied for appearance.

lead: Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) is a thiazide diuretic, a prescription medicine that makes the kidneys excrete more sodium and water. It is used to treat high blood pressure and edema from heart failure and other conditions, and sometimes to reduce kidney stone recurrence. It became commercially available in 1959, is on the WHO Essential Medicines List, and was the 18th most prescribed drug in the US in 2024, with more than 31 million prescriptions, according to Wikipedia [1].

In looksmaxxing forums, people discuss water-retention drugs as a way to look leaner and less puffy, since fluid held under the skin can blur the jawline and cheeks. The chain proponents describe is straightforward: more sodium and water leave in the urine, less fluid is retained, and facial and body definition look sharper. Members have asked whether HCTZ is a safer alternative to the loop diuretic furosemide (Lasix) that can be used every day [2]. Forum threads contain few first-hand reports, and no published study has examined it for facial depuffing or other cosmetic purposes.

Clinically HCTZ acts on the distal convoluted tubule. Commonly reported adverse effects are electrolyte disturbances, raised uric acid and blood glucose, and photosensitivity; Australian and US regulators updated its labelling for non-melanoma skin cancer risk in 2020, and the IARC classified it as a Group 1 carcinogen in November 2024 [1]. It is prescription-only in most countries and prohibited in sport by WADA [1].
infobox: Non-melanoma skin cancer label changes (2020); IARC Group 1 (2024) [1]

paras: HCTZ is used for hypertension, edema, congestive heart failure, diabetes insipidus, renal tubular acidosis and prevention of calcium kidney stones in people with high urinary calcium. Off-label uses include osteopenia, hypoparathyroidism, Dent's disease and Meniere disease, with low-quality, mostly observational evidence for bone benefits [1]. It is frequently combined with other agents such as ACE inhibitors, as in lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide tablets, and Wikipedia lists fixed-dose combinations with ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, beta-blockers and triamterene [1][3]. Wikipedia says it can be used as initial monotherapy for hypertension, with choice weighing long-term metabolic effects [1].

Looksmax.org members have discussed diuretics for water retention, and a thread asks how HCTZ compares with Lasix, which is a loop diuretic. The theory is that a thiazide usable every day is a safer alternative to a stronger drug. A reply asks how daily use would be better than a 40 mg Lasix dose, and the original poster asks for first-hand experience and tags several members [2].

Wikipedia's article on diuretics describes the broader misuse patterns recorded for the drug class: athletes use them to dilute doping agents and make weight in sports such as boxing and wrestling, and people with eating disorders, especially bulimia nervosa, use them for weight loss; the article does not discuss cosmetic depuffing [4].

Wikipedia describes thiazides and thiazide-like drugs such as chlorthalidone and indapamide as acting in the distal convoluted tubule with a low-ceiling dose response, whereas loop diuretics such as furosemide, bumetanide and torsemide act in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle and can cause large diuresis [4][5]. Furosemide (Lasix) acts faster: oral effect begins within 30 to 60 minutes, with diuresis usually complete within 6 to 8 hours, and its elimination half-life is about 2 hours [6]. HCTZ acts within about 2 hours, peaks around 4 hours and lasts about 6 to 12 hours [1].

Wikipedia notes that furosemide patents date to 1959 with medical approval in 1964, and that WADA lists it as banned because it may mask other drugs, as it does HCTZ [6][1]. Its documented adverse effects include electrolyte abnormalities, low blood pressure, gout via raised uric acid, high blood sugar and, in some reports, hearing loss, and monitoring of electrolytes and kidney function is recommended in clinical use [6].

The ACCOMPLISH trial compared benazepril with amlodipine against benazepril with hydrochlorothiazide in high-risk hypertensive patients [7]. An earlier MRC trial in older adults examined thiazide-based treatment of hypertension [8]. A 2022 pragmatic VA trial randomised 13,523 patients aged 65 or older who were already on hydrochlorothiazide to continue it or switch to chlorthalidone; at a median 2.4 years, primary cardiovascular outcomes were 10.4% with chlorthalidone and 10.0% with HCTZ (hazard ratio 1.04) [9]. A secondary analysis examined kidney outcomes [10].

Wikipedia cites a 2018 Cochrane review reporting that doses of 50 mg or less over four years reduced mortality and cardiovascular disease compared with higher doses or beta-blockers, a 2019 Lancet analysis finding thiazide-type diuretics had better effectiveness and safety profiles than ACE inhibitors and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers as initial monotherapy, and notes that chlorthalidone is more potent [1]. In kidney stone prevention, a double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial tested hydrochlorothiazide in patients with recurrent calcium-containing stones [11].

Reported effects include low potassium, magnesium and sodium; high calcium, uric acid (with gout risk), blood sugar and lipids; headache, nausea, vomiting, photosensitivity, weight gain and pancreatitis [1]. Low potassium is described as the most important adverse effect of thiazides as a class, and can be mitigated clinically with potassium supplements or potassium-sparing combinations [1][5]. Evidence for cross-reactivity in people with sulfa allergy is weak; Wikipedia cites a 2003 NEJM study suggesting risk tracks general allergic predisposition rather than sulfonamide cross-reactivity [1]. Case reports describe skin reactions such as cutaneous pseudolymphoma [12].

Australia's TGA and the US FDA updated labelling for non-melanoma skin cancer risk in August 2020, and in November 2024 the IARC classified HCTZ as a Group 1 carcinogen, alongside voriconazole and tacrolimus [1]. Diuretics affect fluid and electrolyte balance, so the electrolyte effects apply to anyone taking them, including without a prescription [4].

HCTZ blocks the sodium-chloride cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule, lowering blood volume through greater urine output; the long-term blood-pressure effect is also thought to involve reduced peripheral vascular resistance, though the mechanism is not fully clear [1][5]. Thiazides also increase calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule, which lowers urinary calcium and underlies their use in calcium stones [5].

It acts within about 2 hours and peaks around 4 hours. Bioavailability is about 70%, it is minimally metabolised and more than 95% is excreted unchanged in urine, with a half-life of roughly 6-15 hours; severe kidney impairment reduces its effectiveness [1]. Pharmacokinetic studies have looked at HCTZ after bariatric surgery and in combinations with valsartan or irbesartan [13].

Wikipedia's thiazide article credits Merck scientists Karl H. Beyer, James M. Sprague, John E. Baer and Frederick C. Novello with developing the thiazides in the 1950s; chlorothiazide, the first in the class, was marketed as Diuril in 1958, and the discovery later received a Lasker Foundation Public Health Award in 1975 [5]. Merck and Ciba Specialty Chemicals both claim the discovery of hydrochlorothiazide, which became commercially available in 1959 [1].
Thiazides then became first-line agents in major hypertension trials of the 1980s and 1990s, including the MRC older-adult trial [8]. HCTZ is now generic and relatively affordable [1].

HCTZ is prescription-only in most countries [1]. The World Anti-Doping Agency prohibits it because diuretics can mask other drugs; Wikipedia notes marathoner Ruth Chepng'etich received a three-year ban from the Athletics Integrity Unit on 23 October 2025 for its presence and use [1]. A registered study generated HCTZ-positive samples for anti-doping control [14].

A looksmax.org thread titled around HCTZ being a safer and better alternative to furosemide asks whether anyone has experience taking it and says it can be used every day; a reply questions how it would be safer or better than a Lasix dose [2]. Experience reports in these threads are sparse, and the discussion centres on whether a milder thiazide is a more sustainable way to manage water retention than a loop diuretic.

No studies found on hydrochlorothiazide for facial depuffing or other appearance goals. In hypertension, trials include ACCOMPLISH, the MRC older-adult trial, a 13,523-patient comparison with chlorthalidone and a registered two-participant comparison with lisinopril [7][8][15][9]. A kidney-stone recurrence trial and many pharmacokinetic studies of combination products also exist [11][13].

lore.intro: Hydrochlorothiazide appears in looksmax.org threads as a candidate daily water-retention drug that members compare with Lasix.[2]

claims.claim: HCTZ is a safer, better alternative to furosemide for water retention.
A mild diuretic can make the face look leaner.
HCTZ can be used every day without the downsides of a stronger water pill.
Thiazides are the milder choice compared with loop diuretics.

The Lasker Foundation recognises the discovery of the thiazides.[5]
